nameStory: Carey's Smartweed honors William Carey, a 19th-century botanist who collected plants in the northeastern United States. Like other smartweeds, it gets the 'smart' part of its name from the peppery, burning taste of its leaves - they're definitely 'smart' enough to make your mouth tingle if you nibble them!
description: Carey's Smartweed is a slender annual herb that grows 1-3 feet tall in wet, sandy areas. It has narrow, lance-shaped leaves and produces small clusters of tiny pink or white flowers along thin, upright stems. This delicate-looking plant is actually quite rare in New England, making it a special find for plant enthusiasts. Its overall appearance is wispy and graceful, often overlooked among other wetland vegetation.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that are 2-4 inches long and taper to a point. They feel smooth to the touch and have a slightly peppery smell when crushed. Look for the papery sheaths (called ocrea) that wrap around the stem where each leaf attaches.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink or white flowers arranged in loose, open clusters at the tips of branches. Each flower is only about 1/8 inch across with 5 petals. The flower clusters feel delicate and sparse compared to other smartweeds.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a slender, branching annual that reaches 1-3 feet tall. The stems are thin and somewhat weak, often leaning on nearby plants for support. The overall appearance is open and airy.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, shiny brown or black seeds that are lens-shaped and about 1/8 inch long. They develop in late summer and fall, often persisting on the dried stems.

habitat: Carey's Smartweed grows in wet, sandy soils along pond shores, stream edges, and seasonal wetlands. It prefers areas that flood in spring but may dry out partially in summer. Look for it in open, sunny spots where competition from taller plants is limited.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge in late spring as small rosettes of narrow leaves. Early growth is often submerged or in very wet soil.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height and begin flowering in mid to late summer. The delicate pink or white flower clusters appear from July through August.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and the plant begins to turn brown. Dried stems may persist with seed clusters still attached.
seasonality.winter: Only dried, brown stem fragments remain, usually broken down by winter weather.

funFact: Carey's Smartweed is so rare in New England that it's been recorded only 8 times - making it one of the region's botanical 'unicorns' that even experienced botanists rarely encounter in the wild!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other rare smartweeds like low smartweed, but Carey's has more open, sparse flower clusters and tends to grow in sandier soils. The combination of very narrow leaves and loose flower arrangements helps distinguish it from the more common, dense-flowered smartweeds.
contextualKnowledge: The smartweed group can be challenging even for experts because many species hybridize and have variable characteristics. Carey's Smartweed is considered a species of conservation concern in New England due to habitat loss from development and wetland destruction.
compareHints: Carey's Smartweed differs from its common cousin spotted lady's thumb by having much sparser, more open flower clusters and lacking the dark triangular spots on the leaves. Unlike the robust swamp smartweed, Carey's is delicate and slender with a more open branching pattern. The rare pale smartweed is similar but typically grows in muddier rather than sandy soils.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many smartweeds, low smartweed stands out for its distinctly bristly leaf sheaths and sprawling, ground-hugging habit - most other smartweeds grow more upright.

American jumpseed is unique among New England's Persicaria species for its woodland habitat preference - nearly all its relatives prefer sunny, wet areas like marshes, pond edges, or disturbed ground.
Among its smartweed relatives, arrow-leaved tearthumb is unique for its arrowhead-shaped leaves - most other Persicaria species have lance-shaped or oval leaves.

Among its many Persicaria relatives in New England, halberd-leaved tearthumb is unique for its climbing habit and distinctive leaf shape - most other smartweeds and knotweeds are upright plants with oval or lance-shaped leaves.
Far Eastern smartweed differs from spotted lady's thumb by having longer, more cylindrical flower clusters rather than short oval ones.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, water smartweed is unique in its amphibious lifestyle and dramatically different leaf forms.
Among its many Persicaria relatives in New England, spotted lady's thumb is one of the easiest to identify thanks to its distinctive dark leaf spots - most other smartweeds lack this feature.

Mile-a-minute differs from its native relatives like arrow-leaved tearthumb and halberd-leaved tearthumb primarily in leaf shape - it has equilateral triangular leaves while the others have arrow or halberd-shaped leaves with distinct pointed lobes.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, pinkweed stands out with its particularly dense, cylindrical flower clusters and robust growth habit.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, pale smartweed stands out for its consistently pale flowers - most other smartweeds have brighter pink blooms.
Among New England's many smartweeds, swamp smartweed stands out for its mild taste and preference for the wettest spots.
Among the many Persicaria species in New England, Asian jumpseed stands out for its delicate, thin growth habit and light green leaves with brown spots.
Among its many smartweed relatives, dotted smartweed is distinguished by those translucent leaf dots and its preference for very wet conditions.
Among its many Persicaria relatives in New England, waterpepper stands out for its intensely peppery taste and drooping flower spikes.
Among the many Persicaria species in New England, Nepal persicaria is distinguished by its relatively recent arrival and limited distribution.
Puritan Smartweed differs from other New England smartweeds by its preference for sandy rather than muddy habitats and its extremely limited distribution.

Among its knotweed relatives, kiss-me-over-the-garden-gate stands out dramatically with its large size and distinctive drooping flower spikes - most other Persicaria species have much smaller, upright flower clusters.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, small water-pepper stands out for its truly diminutive size and exceptionally short flower clusters.
Among New England's smartweeds, bog smartweed's thread-like leaves are diagnostic – no other Persicaria species has such narrow foliage.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, Asian lady's thumb stands out for its low, mat-forming growth habit rather than the upright stance of most smartweeds.
Among New England's many smartweeds, stout smartweed lives up to its name with the thickest, most substantial stems in the genus.

Among New England's many Persicaria species, dense-flowered smartweed stands out for its exceptionally compact, bottlebrush-like flower spikes - much denser than the looser clusters of spotted lady's thumb or pinkweed.

Among New England's many Persicaria species, Japanese indigo is most similar to spotted lady's thumb and pinkweed in overall appearance, but it's much rarer and has a more upright, less sprawling growth habit.
